title: 1838 Mormon War

text:
The 1838 Mormon War (or Missouri Mormon War) was a period of civil unrest in northern Missouri during the summer and fall of 1838, beginning with local vigilante clashes, and concluding with the state-mandated expulsion or extermination of Mormons (Latter Day Saints) from the state.
Tensions originated in 1831 when, driven by revelations to "gather," Mormons established a settlement in Jackson County, Missouri, while maintaining their main headquarters in Kirtland, Ohio. Local mobs violently expelled them from Jackson County two years later. Seeking a permanent compromise, the Missouri legislature created Caldwell County in 1836, intending to confine Mormon settlement. However, the 1837 collapse of the Ohio headquarters triggered a wave of migration to the region, reigniting local anxieties over Mormon political and economic expansion. 
A brawl erupted on August 6 when a crowd blocked Mormons from voting in Gallatin. In September, anti-Mormon vigilantes besieged the Mormon town of De Witt. Governor Lilburn Boggs refused to intervene, declaring the quarrel was "between the Mormons and the mob." Following the fall of De Witt, the vigilantes marched into Daviess County to continue their campaign. Left to their own defense, Mormons mobilized their state-commissioned militia and the Danite network to launch retaliatory raids. Following the Battle of Crooked River, Boggs declared the Mormons in open rebellion and issued Missouri Executive Order 44, mandating their expulsion or extermination. 
Days later, a rogue militia massacred 17 unarmed Mormons at Hawn's Mill. Mormons surrendered at Far West on November 1. Although a court-martial sentenced Mormon founder Joseph Smith and others to execution by firing squad for treason, Brigadier General Alexander Doniphan defied the command, denouncing it as "cold-blooded murder." Smith was instead imprisoned in Liberty Jail until guards allowed his escape in April 1839, joining 10,000 displaced Mormons seeking refuge in Illinois.
